name: Cerebellar tonsil
summary: The rounded lobules on the inferomedial surface of each hemisphere that sit directly above the foramen magnum on either side of the medulla. They matter almost entirely because of where they are: raised pressure in the posterior fossa pushes them into the foramen magnum (tonsillar herniation), compressing the medulla and blocking CSF flow, and the Chiari I malformation is defined by their congenital descent below the foramen magnum.

anatomy.location: Inferomedial cerebellar hemisphere adjacent to the vallecula, lateral to the uvula and above the foramen magnum, bounded above by the biventral lobule; normally the tonsillar tips lie at or above the plane of the foramen magnum (McRae line).

function: Part of the posterior lobe (hemispheric lobule IX); no unique clinical function, but a critical space-occupying landmark at the craniocervical junction.

bestView.label: tonsil above the foramen magnum on a parasagittal slice

imaging.normalAppearance: On sagittal T1 the tonsillar tip should not lie more than about 5 mm below the line from the basion to the opisthion; peg-like pointed tonsils with obliteration of the cisterna magna indicate Chiari I. Rounded tonsils forced down acutely with effaced CSF indicate herniation.

pathology.finding: Tonsils crowded into the foramen magnum with obliterated basal cisterns and cisterna magna, often with a posterior fossa mass or diffuse swelling; lumbar puncture is contraindicated.
Pointed tonsils more than 5 mm below the foramen magnum with a small posterior fossa, often with a cervical syrinx; look for the syrinx on sagittal T2.
Mild tonsillar descent with brainstem sagging, dural enhancement and subdural collections, reversible after treatment.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal T1/T2 of the craniocervical junction; CT in the emergency setting

lesionEffects.deficit: Neck pain, occipital headache worse with cough or strain
lesionEffects.mechanism: Tonsillar impaction at the foramen magnum (Chiari)

lesionEffects.deficit: Respiratory arrest, bradycardia, hypertension and coma
lesionEffects.mechanism: Acute medullary compression by herniating tonsils

lesionEffects.deficit: Syringomyelia with cape-like dissociated sensory loss
lesionEffects.mechanism: Disturbed CSF dynamics at the foramen magnum in Chiari I

examination: Downbeat nystagmus, lower cranial nerve function
Sensory testing for a syrinx pattern
In a deteriorating patient: breathing pattern, pulse and blood pressure (Cushing response)
pearls: Never perform a lumbar puncture when the tonsils are crowded into the foramen magnum on imaging
Cough headache in a young adult with downbeat nystagmus should prompt a sagittal MRI of the craniocervical junction
